title: The Replication Problem
text:
Replication studies have become a central tool for evaluating whether published findings hold up under scrutiny. In a recent project, a team of researchers attempted to reproduce the results of 100 psychology experiments, using the same methods as the original authors. Only about a third of the original effects were reliably reproduced, although the replicated effects tended to be smaller than those first reported. The authors argued that this gap reflects not fraud but the difficulty of distinguishing genuine effects from statistical noise.

Critics, however, caution against interpreting a single failed replication as proof that an original finding is false. Small sample sizes, subtle differences in procedure, and variation between populations can all produce discrepant outcomes. For this reason, many scientists now favour large, multi-site replications, which pool data across laboratories and provide more precise estimates of effect size. Such efforts are expensive, yet they offer a more reliable basis for scientific consensus.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what did the team of researchers attempt to do?
options: Reproduce the results of 100 psychology experiments
Measure how funding affects research quality
Publish a review of replication journals

questions.text: According to paragraph two, what can produce discrepant outcomes in replication?
options: Small sample sizes and subtle procedural differences

questions.text: What can be inferred about why the replicated effects were smaller than the originally reported effects?
options: The original researchers deliberately exaggerated their results
Initial studies may have overestimated effects partly because of statistical noise
Replication methods are always more accurate than original methods
The effects were not real at all

questions.text: What is the author's most likely attitude toward large, multi-site replications?
options: Skeptical, because they are too cheap to be meaningful
Favourable, because they give more reliable estimates despite their cost
Indifferent, because they add nothing to scientific knowledge
Opposed, because they discourage collaboration between laboratories

paragraph_translations: Estudos de replicação tornaram-se uma ferramenta central para avaliar se os resultados publicados se sustentam sob escrutínio. Em um projeto recente, uma equipe de pesquisadores tentou reproduzir os resultados de 100 experimentos de psicologia, usando os mesmos métodos dos autores originais. Apenas cerca de um terço dos efeitos originais foi reproduzido de forma confiável, embora os efeitos replicados tendessem a ser menores do que os relatados inicialmente. Os autores argumentaram que essa diferença reflete não fraude, mas a dificuldade de distinguir efeitos genuínos de ruído estatístico.

Críticos, porém, alertam contra interpretar uma única falha de replicação como prova de que um achado original é falso. Amostras pequenas, diferenças sutis de procedimento e variação entre populações podem produzir resultados discrepantes. Por isso, muitos cientistas hoje preferem replicações grandes e em vários locais, que reúnem dados de diversos laboratórios e fornecem estimativas mais precisas do tamanho do efeito. Esses esforços são caros, mas oferecem uma base mais confiável para o consenso científico.
